title: Leaving their beds
hook: they forsake their beds to call on their Lord in fear and hope (32:16)

segments.voice: Yesterday, if the sea were ink, and your line was the words don't run out. Did you add a second word to your scrap of paper before sleep? Day five hundred thirty-seven, and a new surah.

There's a particular quiet at about four in the morning. No traffic. No notifications. The fridge hums. A bird tries one note and stops. Shift workers know it, new parents know it, and so do people who get up on purpose, before dawn, to pray. Surah As-Sajdah, the Prostration, the thirty-second, is short, and it describes the believers in a single picture that has nothing to do with crowds or mosques. It's a picture of someone alone, at night, getting out of a warm bed.

The verse before describes those who, when reminded of God's signs, fall down in prostration; it's one of the places in the Qur'an where many Muslims prostrate as they recite, which is how the surah got its name. Then the picture. Pickthall: "Who forsake their beds to cry unto their Lord in fear and hope". The Arabic is vivid: tatajafa junubuhum 'an al-madaji', their sides draw away from their beds. As if the body itself pulls back from sleep. And notice the two words: fear and hope, khawfan wa tama'an. Not one or the other. The night prayer holds both, the honesty about what's wrong and the reaching toward mercy. The practice is called qiyam al-layl, standing in the night. Another name is tahajjud, from a root that means waking from sleep. A hadith in Tirmidhi says the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, explaining to Mu'adh ibn Jabal the doors of good, mentioned a person's prayer in the middle of the night, and then recited this very verse. And a hadith in Bukhari and Muslim says that in the last third of every night, God descends to the nearest heaven and asks: who is calling on Me, that I may answer him? Who is asking of Me, that I may give him? It's voluntary, not one of the five prayers. Many people do it only sometimes, a few short units, two or four or more, in the dark. The Prophet, it's reported, recited this surah before sleeping. So the verse is about the cost: a warm bed, a little sleep. And what's bought with it is a conversation nobody else hears.
screen: `THEIR SIDES DRAW AWAY FROM THEIR BEDS.` · `IN FEAR AND IN HOPE.` · `QIYAM AL-LAYL, TAHAJJUD.` · `THE LAST THIRD OF THE NIGHT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: wake briefly before dawn. Sit, and let the breath settle. Picture tonight. If it's safe and sensible for your sleep, decide to set an alarm a little before dawn, even fifteen minutes before you'd normally rise. Picture the quiet, the dark room, the cold floor. Picture sitting up and doing one small thing with that time: if you pray, two short units of prayer, or a few words of your own; if you don't, a few minutes of stillness and gratitude. Then back to sleep, or into the day. The bell holds the time.
Qiyam al-layl. Standing in the night: the voluntary prayer of people whose sides draw away from their beds, in fear and hope. Today's word.
Your line: up in the night. Tonight, set the alarm you pictured, and put it where you'll have to sit up to reach it. Day five hundred thirty-seven.

howItsDone: Many Muslims pray tahajjud, voluntary night prayer, in the last part of the night before the dawn prayer, especially in Ramadan, and many recite Surah As-Sajdah before sleeping.

original.note: Arabic: standing in the night, the voluntary night prayer, also called tahajjud.

trapdoor: what you thought: praying when you can't sleep.
what it means: getting up on purpose, in the dark, to speak to God in fear and hope, when nobody else is watching.
what a scholar hears: tatajafa junubuhum 'an al-madaji' in 32:16; Mu'adh's hadith in Tirmidhi 2616; and the descent in the last third of the night in Bukhari 1145.
